**The meta-learner must see the kind of base-model predictions it will receive at deployment.** A highly flexible base model may predict its own training labels nearly perfectly while generalizing poorly. If those in-sample predictions train the stacker, the stacker learns to trust an unrealistic signal. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html)

Split training data into folds. For each fold, fit each base model on the other folds and predict the held-out rows. Collect those out-of-fold predictions into a new feature table and fit the meta-model there. Every meta-training row now contains predictions from models that did not train on that row.

Then refit base models on the permitted full training set for serving, while evaluating the entire stack on an independent holdout. Preprocessing and hyperparameter choices must respect the same fold boundaries.

**The failure is leakage, not a guaranteed 100% weight outcome.** A stacker might distribute weights in many ways, but in-sample inputs bias its evidence. Use time-aware or group-aware folds when deployment requires them. Otherwise closely related records can leak even though the row itself was technically held out.

**Technical details and references.**

Stacking trains a second-level model on predictions from several base learners. Training it on in-sample predictions lets it exploit overfitting patterns unavailable at deployment. Generate each training row's base predictions from models fitted without that row, using group/time-aware folds when needed. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html)

Fit the meta-model on those out-of-fold features, then refit base models on allowed training data for serving. In-sample stacking does not literally always assign 100% weight to one model; the real issue is biased meta-training information. Keep preprocessing within folds and reserve an independent evaluation set for the entire stacked pipeline.
